title: The chance it does not happen
objectives: Use the complement to turn a hard count into an easy one.
Find the chance of at least one success as one minus the chance of none.

screens.prose: Toss a fair coin three times. Each of the 8 paths is equally likely.
screens.question: Tap every path with at least one head.

hints.text: “At least one head” means one, two or three heads.
Only one path has no head at all.
Tap every path except TTT.

feedback.correct: Seven paths: every path except TTT.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap each path that has an H anywhere in it.

byKey.exactly-one: Those have exactly one head. “At least one” also takes two or three.
byKey.no-hhh: You missed HHH. Three heads is at least one head.
byKey.t-t-t: TTT has no heads at all.
byKey.h-h-h: You missed HHH. Three heads is at least one head.
byKey.h-h-t: You missed HHT. Two heads is at least one.
byKey.h-t-h: You missed HTH. Two heads is at least one.
byKey.t-h-h: You missed THH. Two heads is at least one.
byKey.h-t-t: You missed HTT. One head is enough.
byKey.t-h-t: You missed THT. One head is enough.
byKey.t-t-h: You missed TTH. One head is enough.

explain.text: You tapped 7 paths, and only TTT was left out. So $P(\text{at least one head}) = \tfrac{7}{8}$. The quick way is to count the one path you skipped: $1 - \tfrac{1}{8}$.

screens.prose: Now roll one fair die again and again. Move the slider to change the number of rolls. The dot shows the chance of at least one six.

derive.caption: Rolls: {{p1.x}}. Chance of at least one six: {{fixed(1 - pow(5/6, p1.x), 4)}}

screens.question: What is the smallest number of rolls that makes at least one six more likely than not?

widget.label: Number of rolls
widget.accept: 4: the chance is 0.4213 at 3 rolls and 0.5177 at 4.

hints.text: Move the slider one roll at a time and read the caption.
Compare the dot with the dashed line at $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
At 3 rolls the chance is 0.4213; at 4 it is 0.5177.

feedback.correct: Four rolls: the chance first passes $\tfrac{1}{2}$ at 0.5177.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the first number of rolls where the dot is above the dashed line.

byKey.adding: You may have added $\tfrac{1}{6}$ per roll: $3 \times \tfrac{1}{6} = \tfrac{1}{2}$. The dot at 3 rolls reads 0.4213.
byKey.six: Six rolls give 0.6651, above $\tfrac{1}{2}$, but fewer rolls already do it.

explain.text: The chance passes $\tfrac{1}{2}$ at 4 rolls, with 0.5177. It keeps climbing but never reaches 1, even at 24 rolls. Next we see where these numbers come from.

screens.prose: In the coin tree, “no heads” held the one path you skipped. It is the complement of “at least one head”, as in the counting course: every outcome is in exactly one of the two. So $$P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none}).$$
screens.question: Four fair tosses. What is $P(\text{at least one head})$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: How many paths have no head at all?
Only this path has no head.
16 paths, and one has no head: $1 - \tfrac{1}{16}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $P(\text{no heads})$ first, then take it from 1.

byKey.none: That is the chance of no heads, TTTT. Take it from 1.
byKey.adding: You added $\tfrac{1}{2}$ four times and passed 1. A chance can never exceed 1.
byKey.three: That is three tosses. Four tosses give 16 paths, and only TTTT has no head.
byKey.half: That is the chance for one toss. More tosses make a head more likely.

explain.text: Four tosses make $2^4 = 16$ equally likely paths, and only TTTT has no head. So $P(\text{at least one head}) = 1 - \tfrac{1}{16} = \tfrac{15}{16}$. Counting the 15 directly takes far longer.

screens.prose: Back to the die, rolled four times. An outcome is a list of four faces, such as 3, 6, 1, 6. There are $6^4 = 1296$ outcomes, all equally likely.
screens.question: How many of the 1296 outcomes contain no six?

hints.text: With no six allowed, how many faces can each roll show?
Read the No six row.
$5 \times 5 \times 5 \times 5 = 5^4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each roll has 5 faces left, and the choices multiply.

byKey.at-least: That counts outcomes with at least one six. We want the ones with none.
byKey.added: You added 5 four times. Each roll's 5 faces pair with every choice on the others, so multiply.
byKey.minus-four: You took away only 4 outcomes, one per roll. Hundreds of outcomes contain a six.
byKey.minus-one-roll: You took away the $6^3 = 216$ outcomes with a six on one roll. A six can be on any roll.

explain.text: Each roll can show 1 to 5, so $5^4 = 625$ outcomes have no six. That leaves $1296 - 625 = 671$ with at least one six.

screens.prose: So 625 of the 1296 equally likely outcomes have no six.
screens.question: What is $P(\text{at least one six in four rolls})$? Give a fraction or a decimal to 4 places.

widget.label: P(at least one six)
widget.accept: Any form equal to $\tfrac{671}{1296}$, or 0.5177 to 4 places.

hints.text: What is $P(\text{no six})$?
625 of the 1296 outcomes have no six.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $P(\text{no six})$, then take it from 1.

byKey.none: That is $P(\text{no six}) = \tfrac{625}{1296}$. Take it from 1.
byKey.adding: You added $\tfrac{1}{6}$ four times. The next screen shows why that overcounts.
byKey.one: That is the chance for one roll. Four rolls give more chances of a six.

explain.text: $P(\text{no six}) = \tfrac{625}{1296} = \left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^4$. So $P(\text{at least one six}) = 1 - \left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^4 = \tfrac{671}{1296} \approx 0.5177$. That matches the dot at 4 rolls.

screens.prose: Sam says each roll gives a six with chance $\tfrac{1}{6}$, so four rolls give $4 \times \tfrac{1}{6} = \tfrac{2}{3}$. Test his method on two rolls, where we can see every outcome.

state.caption: Row 6: a six first. Column 6: a six second.

screens.question: Sam's method gives $\tfrac{2}{6} = \tfrac{12}{36}$ for two rolls. What is the true $P(\text{at least one six})$?

options.why: You added the row and the column. The cell (6, 6) is in both, so it was counted twice.
That is the chance of no six: the unshaded cells.
That is one roll. The second roll adds more ways to see a six.

hints.text: How many shaded cells are there, counting each cell once?
This cell is in the row and in the column.
Row 6 has 6 cells and column 6 has 6. They share (6, 6), so $6 + 6 - 1 = 11$. Or: $36 - 25 = 11$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the shaded cells, each one once.

byKey.sam: You added the row and the column, as Sam did. The cell (6, 6) is in both, so it was counted twice.

explain.text: Adding $\tfrac{1}{6}$ per roll counts (6, 6) twice, so it overshoots. With four rolls it overshoots more: $\tfrac{2}{3}$ against the true 0.5177. With six rolls it says $\tfrac{6}{6} = 1$, yet six rolls often miss a six.

screens.prose: On the curve, the chance climbed towards 1 but never reached it. When is “at least one” certain?

state.caption: Rolls: 24. Chance of at least one six: 0.9874

derive.caption: Rolls: {{p1.x}}. Chance of at least one six: {{fixed(1 - pow(5/6, p1.x), 4)}}

screens.question: For which of these is $P(\text{at least one}) = 1$ exactly?

options.text: At least one six in 100 rolls of a fair die
options.why: Very close, but $P(\text{no six}) = \left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^{100}$ is above 0. So the chance falls just short of 1.

options.text: At least one six in 6 rolls of a fair die
options.why: Adding $\tfrac{1}{6}$ six times says 1. The true chance is $1 - \left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^6 \approx 0.6651$.

options.text: At least one head in 3 tosses of a coin with heads on both sides
At least one up day in 20 days, when each day is up with chance 0.6
options.why: $P(\text{no up day}) = 0.4^{20}$ is tiny but not 0. The chance is about 0.99999999.

hints.text: At least one is certain only when none is impossible.
Which case has $P(\text{none}) = 0$?
A two-headed coin can never show tails, so “no heads” has chance 0.

feedback.correct: Only the two-headed coin makes “none” impossible.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the case where “none” cannot happen at all.

explain.text: $P(\text{at least one}) = 1$ exactly when $P(\text{none}) = 0$. A two-headed coin never lands tails, so “no heads” is the empty event. Everywhere else “none” stays possible, however small its chance.

screens.prose: Now the rule behind the curve. Roll a fair die $n$ times: $S$ has $6^n$ equally likely outcomes. Of these, $5^n$ have no six. So $$P(\text{no six}) = \frac{5^n}{6^n} = \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^n.$$
screens.question: Write $P(\text{at least one six in } n \text{ rolls})$ in terms of $n$.

widget.label: P(at least one six in n rolls)

hints.text: “At least one six” is the complement of which event?
Use $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none})$.
Take $\left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^n$ from 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the complement of “no six”.

byKey.none: That is $P(\text{no six})$. Take it from 1.
byKey.adding: That adds $\tfrac{1}{6}$ per roll, which counts outcomes with several sixes more than once.
byKey.all-six: $\left(\tfrac{1}{6}\right)^n$ is the chance of all sixes. The complement of at least one six is no six.

explain.text: “At least one six” and “no six” share no outcome and cover $S$. So $P(\text{at least one six}) = 1 - \left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^n$. At $n = 4$ that is 0.5177, the dot on the curve.

screens.prose: A trader has a losing day with chance 0.4, and one day's result never changes the chances on another day. Days like these are called independent, and their chances multiply, just as $\tfrac{5^4}{6^4} = \left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^4$ did. Consider a 5-day week.

state.caption: Each day is independent of the others

screens.question: What is $P(\text{at least one losing day})$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

hints.text: What is the complement of “at least one losing day”?
No losing day means five days that are not losing.
$P(\text{none}) = 0.6^5 = 0.07776$, so take it from 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance of no losing day, then take it from 1.

byKey.adding: You added 0.4 five times and passed 1. A chance cannot exceed 1.
byKey.none: That is $0.6^5$, the chance of no losing day. Take it from 1.
byKey.all: That is $0.4^5$, five losing days in a row. At least one is far more likely.
byKey.wrong-comp: You took the complement of five losing days. The complement of at least one losing day is no losing day.

explain.text: No losing day needs five days that are not losing: $0.6^5 = 0.07776$. So $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - 0.07776 = 0.92224$. A trader who wins 60% of days still has a losing day in most weeks.

screens.prose: You place 10 limit orders in different stocks. Each fills with chance 0.2, independently of the others.
screens.question: What is the chance that none of the 10 orders fills? Give a decimal to 4 places.

hints.text: None fills means every order misses.
One order misses with chance 0.8.
Ten independent misses: $0.8^{10}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the chance of a miss once for each order.

byKey.at-least: That is the chance at least one fills, the complement. The question asks for none.
byKey.one: That is the chance one order misses. All ten must miss.
byKey.all: That is the chance all ten fill.

explain.text: Each order misses with chance 0.8, so all ten miss with chance $0.8^{10} \approx 0.1074$. The complement, at least one fill, has chance about 0.8926. Even ten unlikely orders give a good chance of some fill.

screens.prose: In the 1650s the Chevalier de Méré made two even-money bets. Bet 1: at least one six in 4 rolls of a die. Bet 2: at least one double six in 24 rolls of two dice. Adding chances, both look like $4 \times \tfrac{1}{6} = 24 \times \tfrac{1}{36} = \tfrac{2}{3}$.

state.caption: One roll of two dice: 1 double six in 36

screens.question: What is the chance of winning bet 2? Give a decimal to 4 places.

widget.label: P(at least one double six in 24 rolls)

hints.text: What is the chance one roll of two dice is not a double six?
One cell of the 36 is a double six.
$P(\text{no double six in 24 rolls}) = \left(\tfrac{35}{36}\right)^{24} \approx 0.5086$. Take it from 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the complement: no double six in any of the 24 rolls.

byKey.adding: You added $\tfrac{1}{36}$ twenty-four times. That counts rolls with several double sixes more than once.
byKey.none: That is the chance of no double six. Take it from 1.
byKey.bet-one: That is bet 1. Bet 2 uses two dice, with $\tfrac{35}{36}$ for no double six on each roll.

explain.text: $1 - \left(\tfrac{35}{36}\right)^{24} \approx 0.4914$, just under one half, so bet 2 loses in the long run. Bet 1 wins: $1 - \left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^4 \approx 0.5177$. Adding chances made the two bets look the same.

ideas: An event and its complement share no outcome and cover $S$, so $P(E^c) = 1 - P(E)$.
For “at least one”, count the complement: $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none})$.
With independent tries, $P(\text{none})$ is a product, such as $\left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^n$, and it is 0 only if “none” is impossible.

formula.name: The complement rule
formula.note: For $n$ rolls of a fair die: $P(\text{at least one six}) = 1 - \left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^n$.

summary.trap: Adding $\tfrac{1}{6}$ per roll counts outcomes with several sixes more than once, and passes 1 after six rolls.

quiz.prose: A fair coin is tossed five times.
quiz.question: What is $P(\text{at least one head})$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only one of the 32 paths has no head.

byKey.none: That is the chance of no heads. Take it from 1.
byKey.adding: You added $\tfrac{1}{2}$ five times and passed 1. A chance cannot exceed 1.

explain.text: Five tosses give $2^5 = 32$ equally likely paths, and only TTTTT has no head. So the chance is $1 - \tfrac{1}{32} = \tfrac{31}{32}$.

quiz.prose: A strategy triggers a margin call on any day with chance 0.03, independently of other days.
quiz.question: What is the chance of no margin call in 20 trading days? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the chance of a quiet day once for each day.

byKey.adding: You took $20 \times 0.03$ from 1. Adding the daily chances overcounts; multiply the quiet days instead.
byKey.at-least: That is the chance of at least one margin call. The question asks for none.

explain.text: Each day is quiet with chance 0.97, so 20 quiet days have chance $0.97^{20} \approx 0.5438$. So a margin call within a month is close to a coin flip.

quiz.prose: A fair die is rolled three times.
quiz.question: Which expression equals $P(\text{at least one six})$?

options.why: You added $\tfrac{1}{6}$ per roll. That counts outcomes with two or three sixes more than once.
That is the chance of three sixes, not at least one.
That is the complement of three sixes. The complement of at least one six is no six.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the complement of “no six”.

explain.text: No six in three rolls has chance $\left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^3 = \tfrac{125}{216}$. So $P(\text{at least one six}) = 1 - \tfrac{125}{216} = \tfrac{91}{216} \approx 0.4213$.
